title: Selection, Trial, and Phenotyping Workbook
purpose: Turn selection theory into repeatable records for qualitative and quantitative traits, selection response, replicated trials, morphology/yield phenotyping, and laboratory-guided chemotype selection.

sections.title: Trait Classification and Selection Method
sections.decisionPrompt: Is the trait being measured in a way that matches its actual distribution and biological behavior?

sections.title: Selection Intensity and Response Record

calculations.name: Simple breeder's equation
calculations.limits: This simplified equation depends on the relevance and quality of the heritability estimate, additive genetic assumptions, and comparable environments.

sections.decisionPrompt: Did the progeny response match the predicted direction and magnitude closely enough to support the selection model?

sections.title: Replicated Trial Design and Deviation Log
qualityRules: Define the experimental unit before analysis.
Do not treat multiple measurements from the same plant as independent biological replicates.
Preserve missing, dead, and excluded units with a reason.
sections.decisionPrompt: Could the observed difference plausibly be explained by position, environment, management, or measurement rather than genotype?

sections.title: Morphology, Flowering, and Yield Phenotyping Sheet
sections.decisionPrompt: Are yield and morphology values comparable because stage, sampling position, moisture basis, and rejection rules were controlled?

sections.title: Chemotype and Volatile Laboratory Selection Record
qualityRules: Compare results only when sampling and analytical basis are compatible.
Keep concentration, ratio, and total analyte yield as separate concepts.
Do not treat a single laboratory sample as proof of whole-plant or multi-environment stability.
sections.decisionPrompt: Does the laboratory result support the breeding objective after accounting for sampling position, method, moisture basis, environment, and replicate uncertainty?

qualityRules: Predefine traits and thresholds before reviewing candidate identities when practical.
Keep raw observations separate from interpretation.
Record uncertainty and missingness rather than silently excluding inconvenient data.
Use replicated progeny or family evidence before claiming genetic gain or stability.
Do not confuse statistical significance with practical breeding importance.
